tier_reason: Benchmark code is public in kostya/lexbor bench/ (test-lexbor.cr, test-libxml.cr, test-libxml.rb, test-nokolexbor.rb, build.sh using `crystal build --release --no-debug`, run.sh; Ruby pinned to 2.7.5), and the README names the CPUs (Ryzen 3800x, Apple M1), so it meets A. It is borderline: the Crystal compiler version and the libxml2/lexbor library versions and build flags are not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Ryzen 3800x, same host language (derived from page data): parse, Crystal lexbor 4.75s vs Crystal Crystagiri(libxml2) 14.20s (~3.0x); Ruby Nokolexbor(lexbor) 4.07s vs Ruby Nokogiri(libxml2) 18.67s (~4.6x); CSS select, Nokolexbor 1.80s vs Nokogiri 92.69s (~51x). The cross-language Crystal-lexbor 0.80s vs Ruby-Nokogiri 92.69s CSS ratio (~116x) mixes host languages; there is no Crystal/libxml2 CSS number (Crystagiri column is '-'). Apple M1 (derived from page data): Nokolexbor 3.41s vs Nokogiri 18.22s parse (~5.3x), CSS 1.11s vs 87.21s (~79x); Crystal lexbor 2.77s vs Crystagiri 126.25s parse (~45.6x) is anomalous (see caveats).
corrections.caveats: Third-party benchmark by the author of the Crystal bindings (kostya/lexbor), not the lexbor project, run through Crystal/Ruby bindings; no run date. On M1, Crystagiri(libxml2) takes 126.25s while Nokogiri on the same libxml2 on the same machine takes 18.22s, so the ~45x M1 figure reflects the Crystal/libxml2 binding path, not libxml2 itself. Treat it as an outlier. The >50x CSS ratios come from Nokogiri's CSS path (CSS translated to XPath through Ruby) and are not a pure C-vs-C comparison. The Crystal compiler version and the libxml2/lexbor versions and build flags are not stated. Gumbo test binaries are referenced in bench/run.sh but commented out in bench/build.sh, so Gumbo numbers are not present in the README despite a Gumbo test program existing.

notes: All README numbers match exactly and the derived ratios are arithmetically right. Downgraded only because the headline ratios (116x CSS, 45x M1) are cross-language or anomalous; like-for-like is ~3-5x parse and ~51-79x CSS (Ruby vs Ruby). Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 2,091 stars, last commit 2026-09-22, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: First-party numbers (MD4C author, CommonMark forum post #12, 2017-07-25). The benchmark script is public (gist mity/24822b24d35ef1f998f970965f8c8e53) and the method is described (10 runs, tmpfs, release builds), but the CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 1.4x-7.7x faster than cmark depending on input (md2html vs cmark CLI, mean of 10 runs; derived from page data): long-block-oneline.md 0.0700s vs 0.1000s = 1.43x; cmark-benchinput.md (Pro-Git compilation) 0.3650s vs 0.7060s = 1.93x; many-paragraphs.md 0.0900s vs 0.4860s = 5.4x; many-emphasis.md 0.1100s vs 0.8460s = 7.7x. On cmark-benchinput, heap peak is 262.74MB vs 472.13MB (~1.8x lower) and realloc() calls 36 vs 1,304,578. The author himself calls the memory comparison 'very unfair' because MD4C builds no AST.
corrections.workload: Parse and render to HTML (MD4C md2html vs cmark CLI), 10 runs each with inputs on tmpfs: cmark-benchinput.md (a multi-language Pro-Git book compilation generated by cmark's `make bench`, 110,648,441 bytes ~105.5MB) plus eight synthetic ~1M-repetition files (long blocks, ATX headers, blank lines, emphasis, fenced code, links, paragraphs); wall time plus memusage(1) heap stats on the Pro-Git input.
corrections.caveats: Author-run benchmark (MD4C author, July 2017) against the cmark master of that time (~0.28), never independently reproduced. The script is public in a gist, but the CPU model and compiler flags are not stated. It compares a SAX-style renderer with AST-building cmark: in the author's own follow-up (post #14), an experimental MD4C path that builds a cmark AST narrows the gap to ~1.4-1.5x (0.32s vs 0.46-0.48s on many-atx-headers/many-paragraphs). The ~105MB size belongs to cmark-benchinput.md alone, not to the synthetic files.

notes: The record's range lower bound was overstated: long-block-oneline gives 1.43x, not 1.9x. The workload wrongly attributed the ~105MB size to the synthetic files. last_commit fixed to the latest default-branch (master) commit, 2026-09-17; the 2026-09-20 date was pushed_at, likely from the 'custom' branch. MIT, 1,457 stars, not archived.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark page (pugixml.org/benchmark.html + benchmark-data.js). It states the compiler (MSVC 2015 'all optimizations on') and the CPU (Core i7 @ 2.67GHz, no exact model), but the benchmark harness source is not public: there is no benchmark repo among zeux's repos and none in pugixml's tree. That makes it C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Faster than libxml2 on all nine test files (derived from page data, benchmark-data.js). On x86: vs libxml2 DOM, 4.5x (house.dae 0.556 vs 2.501) to 23.4x (cathedral.xml); vs libxml2 SAX, 2.7x (house.dae 0.556 vs 1.500) to 19.1x (Russian.sml); e.g. English.sml 0.771 vs 6.412 (DOM, 8.3x) and 3.218 (SAX, 4.2x). x64 is similar: DOM 4.1x-24.1x, SAX 2.6x-19.7x.
corrections.caveats: The pugixml.org benchmark page states the compiler (MSVC 2015, 'all optimizations on') and the CPU (Intel Core i7 @ 2.67 GHz, no exact model), but the benchmark harness source is not public (no benchmark repo under the zeux GitHub account), so it falls short of Tier A. There is no run date, and the current release (1.16) postdates the benchmarked version. benchmark-data.js labels values 'us/byte', but the accompanying MB/s figures (e.g. 0.556 -> 1714 Mb/s) match ns/byte. The unit label is wrong; ratios are unaffected.

notes: The record's cited numbers match benchmark-data.js exactly. The two files it cited are the lowest-ratio ones, so the claim was understated, and claimed_speedup is widened to the full range. MIT, 4,651 stars, last commit 2026-06-16, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (benches/xml.rs, benches/Cargo.toml; libxml2 via the feature-gated rust `libxml` crate), but the README gives no CPU model, rustc version or flags, or libxml2 version, so it is first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: `cargo bench --features=libxml` using the `bencher` crate (libtest-style ns/iter output, not criterion); libxml2 called via the rust `libxml` 0.3.1 bindings (Parser::default().parse_string). The rustc version, flags and libxml2 version/build are not stated.
corrections.caveats: Benchmark code is public (benches/xml.rs, not bench/xml.rs), but the README states no CPU model, rustc/libxml2 versions, build flags or date, so it falls short of Tier A. libxml2 is driven through Rust FFI bindings (rust-libxml), so its time includes binding overhead. The README is internally inconsistent: huge_roxmltree is 2,997,887 ns in the libxml2 table but 3,147,424 ns in the quick-xml table, where huge_quick_xml shows exactly 2,997,887 ns (likely a copy-paste slip). The huge-file ratio is ~2.2-2.3x either way.

notes: All four libxml2-vs-roxmltree numbers match the README, and the derived ratios are correct. The license 'Apache-2.0 OR MIT' is confirmed by Cargo.toml ('MIT OR Apache-2.0') and the LICENSE-MIT/LICENSE-APACHE files, even though GitHub's API reports only Apache-2.0. 537 stars, last commit 2026-09-22.

tier_reason: The public benchmark suite benchmarks/c/ (CMakeLists.txt, src/, run.py.in; Google Benchmark) runs re2c against Ragel 7.0.4. It is built with GCC-14.2.0 and Clang-19.1.4 at -O3 -g, flags in CMakeLists.txt RE2C_CXX_FLAGS, on an Intel Core i7-8750H (results/env_20250131.rst), so it meets A.

corrections.license: Public Domain (dedication, not a formal OSI license)
corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed (derived from page data, results_20250131.json cpu_time; re2c-simple vs ragel-simple): real-world formats ~1.0x-1.44x faster (http-rfc7230/gcc 21.2 vs 25.5 = 1.20x; email/gcc 1.32x, email/clang 1.44x; datetime/gcc 1.36x; uri-rfc3986/gcc 1.00x; apache-log/gcc 1.02x). Against Ragel's 'buffered' variant the margin shrinks (http-rfc7230/gcc 21.2 vs 24.2 = 1.14x), and Ragel wins apache-log/gcc (14.0 vs 14.9). On synthetic rep-*/rep-alt-* patterns re2c is 1.5x-4.1x slower (rep-5-rep-3-rep-2/clang 34.4 vs 8.4); several synthetic alt2-*/alt4-*/cat* cases (mostly gcc) also favor Ragel, by up to 1.35x (alt2-8/gcc 17.7 vs 13.1).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC-14.2.0 and Clang-19.1.4 (g++/clang++), -O3 -g -Wall; re2c --reusable --tags -i; Ragel 7.0.4 -G2 (per benchmarks/c/CMakeLists.txt and results/env_20250131.rst)
corrections.workload: Submatch-extraction lexers generated by re2c (--tags) vs Ragel 7 (-G2), Google Benchmark CPU time on 35 benchmarks: real-world formats (HTTP per RFC7230 and a simple variant, URI per RFC3986 and a simple variant, Apache log, datetime-to-JSON, email, IPv4; three taken from the Kleenex repo) plus synthetic alt/cat/rep patterns. Each is built with GCC-14.2.0 and Clang-19.1.4 at -O3.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is Ragel, not Flex/Bison/ANTLR/Boost.Spirit; none of those appear in re2c's benchmark suite. Results are mixed: real-world grammars mostly favor re2c (~1.0-1.44x simple-vs-simple, smaller against Ragel's buffered variant), but synthetic repetition-heavy patterns favor Ragel by 1.5-4.1x, so 'faster' does not hold universally. Ragel has no results for 4 of the 35 benchmarks (rep-cat-*, rep-23-rep-19-rep-17), and the cpu_time unit is not stated in the JSON. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION because the LICENSE is a bespoke public-domain dedication ('re2c is in the public domain... may be distributed freely'), with no patent grant; usability=copyable per the public-domain rule.

notes: The record's cited numbers match the JSON; I added best-variant context and the full slowdown range. Ragel is not a listed category baseline but is a recognizable, widely used incumbent state-machine generator, so baseline_in_list=false stands. License set to the catalog's existing public-domain wording. 1,310 stars, last commit 2026-09-17.
